segs.p: Yadāhaṁ, bhante, upāsikā paṭidesitā nābhijānāmi kiñci sikkhāpadaṁ sañcicca vītikkamitā”ti.
segs.e: Ever since I declared myself a lay follower, I can’t recall deliberately breaking any precept.”
“It’s incredible, Nanda’s Mother, it’s amazing!”

segs.p: “Na kho me, bhante, eseva acchariyo abbhuto dhammo.
segs.e: “Sir, this is not my only incredible and amazing quality;

segs.p: Atthi me aññopi acchariyo abbhuto dhammo.
segs.e: there is another.

segs.p: Idhāhaṁ, bhante, yāvade ākaṅkhāmi vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṁ savicāraṁ vivekajaṁ pītisukhaṁ paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharāmi.
segs.e: Whenever I want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

segs.p: Vitakkavicārānaṁ vūpasamā ajjhattaṁ sampasādanaṁ cetaso ekodibhāvaṁ avitakkaṁ avicāraṁ vivekajaṁ pītisukhaṁ dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharāmi.
segs.e: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, I enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

segs.p: Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhikā ca viharāmi satā ca sampajānā sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṁvedemi, yaṁ taṁ ariyā ācikkhanti: ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharāmi.
segs.e: And with the fading away of rapture, I enter and remain in the third absorption, where I meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

segs.p: Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṁ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṁ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṁ catutthaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharāmī”ti.
segs.e: With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, I enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.”
“It’s incredible, Nanda’s Mother, it’s amazing!”

segs.e: Of the five lower fetters taught by the Buddha, I don’t see any that I haven’t given up.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto nandamātaraṁ upāsikaṁ dhammiyā kathāya sandassetvā samādapetvā samuttejetvā sampahaṁsetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmīti.
segs.e: Then Venerable Sāriputta educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired Nanda’s Mother with a Dhamma talk, after which he rose from his seat and left.
Numbered Discourses 7.54
6. The Undeclared Points
The Undeclared Points

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo yena sutavato ariyasāvakassa vicikicchā nuppajjati abyākatavatthūsū”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why a learned noble disciple has no doubts regarding the undeclared points?”

segs.p: “Diṭṭhinirodhā kho, bhikkhu, sutavato ariyasāvakassa vicikicchā nuppajjati abyākatavatthūsu.
segs.e: “Mendicant, it’s due to the cessation of views that a learned noble disciple has no doubts regarding the undeclared points.

segs.p: ‘Hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, diṭṭhigatametaṁ;
segs.e: ‘A realized one still exists after death’: this is a misconception.

segs.p: ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, diṭṭhigatametaṁ;
segs.e: ‘A realized one no longer exists after death’: this is a misconception.

segs.p: ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, diṭṭhigatametaṁ;
segs.e: ‘A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death’: this is a misconception.

segs.p: ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, diṭṭhigatametaṁ.
segs.e: ‘A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death’: this is a misconception.

segs.p: Assutavā, bhikkhu, puthujjano diṭṭhiṁ nappajānāti, diṭṭhisamudayaṁ nappajānāti, diṭṭhinirodhaṁ nappajānāti, diṭṭhinirodhagāminiṁ paṭipadaṁ nappajānāti.
segs.e: An unlearned ordinary person doesn’t understand views, their origin, their cessation, or the practice that leads to their cessation.

segs.p: Tassa sā diṭṭhi pavaḍḍhati, so na parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Na parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: And so their views grow. They’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

segs.p: Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhu, ariyasāvako diṭṭhiṁ pajānāti, diṭṭhisamudayaṁ pajānāti, diṭṭhinirodhaṁ pajānāti, diṭṭhinirodhagāminiṁ paṭipadaṁ pajānāti.
segs.e: A learned noble disciple does understand views, their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation.

segs.p: Tassa sā diṭṭhi nirujjhati, so parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: And so their views cease. They’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They’re freed from suffering, I say.

segs.p: Evaṁ jānaṁ kho, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako evaṁ passaṁ ‘hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’tipi na byākaroti;
segs.e: Knowing and seeing this, a learned noble disciple does not answer: ‘A realized one still exists after death’,

segs.p: ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’tipi na byākaroti;
segs.e: ‘A realized one no longer exists after death’,

segs.p: ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’tipi na byākaroti;
segs.e: ‘A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death’,

segs.p: ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’tipi na byākaroti.
segs.e: ‘A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death.’

segs.p: Evaṁ jānaṁ kho, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako evaṁ passaṁ evaṁ abyākaraṇadhammo hoti abyākatavatthūsu.
segs.e: Knowing and seeing this, a learned noble disciple does not declare the undeclared points.

segs.p: Evaṁ jānaṁ kho, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako evaṁ passaṁ na chambhati, na kampati, na vedhati, na santāsaṁ āpajjati abyākatavatthūsu.
segs.e: Knowing and seeing this, a learned noble disciple doesn’t shake, tremble, quake, or get nervous regarding the undeclared points.

segs.p: ‘Hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, taṇhāgatametaṁ …pe…
segs.e: ‘A realized one still exists after death’: this is just about craving. …
it’s just about perception …
it’s a conceiving …
it’s a proliferation …
it’s just about grasping …

segs.p: ‘hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, vippaṭisāro eso;
segs.e: ‘A realized one still exists after death’: this is a regret.

segs.p: ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, vippaṭisāro eso;
segs.e: ‘A realized one no longer exists after death’: this is a regret.

segs.p: ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, vippaṭisāro eso;
segs.e: ‘A realized one both still exists and no longer exists after death’: this is a regret.

segs.p: ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti kho, bhikkhu, vippaṭisāro eso.
segs.e: ‘A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death’: this is a regret.

segs.p: Assutavā, bhikkhu, puthujjano vippaṭisāraṁ nappajānāti, vippaṭisārasamudayaṁ nappajānāti, vippaṭisāranirodhaṁ nappajānāti, vippaṭisāranirodhagāminiṁ paṭipadaṁ nappajānāti.
segs.e: An unlearned ordinary person doesn’t understand regrets, their origin, their cessation, or the practice that leads to their cessation.

segs.p: Tassa so vippaṭisāro pavaḍḍhati, so na parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. ‘Na parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: And so their regrets grow. They’re not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They’re not freed from suffering, I say.

segs.p: Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhu, ariyasāvako vippaṭisāraṁ pajānāti, vippaṭisārasamudayaṁ pajānāti, vippaṭisāranirodhaṁ pajānāti, vippaṭisāranirodhagāminiṁ paṭipadaṁ pajānāti.
segs.e: A learned noble disciple does understand regrets, their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation.

segs.p: Tassa so vippaṭisāro nirujjhati, so parimuccati jātiyā …pe… ‘… dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: And so their regrets cease. They’re freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They’re freed from suffering, I say.

segs.p: Evaṁ jānaṁ kho, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako evaṁ passaṁ ‘hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’tipi na byākaroti …pe…
segs.e: Knowing and seeing this, a learned noble disciple does not answer: ‘A realized one still exists after death’ …

segs.p: ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’tipi na byākaroti.
segs.e: ‘A realized one neither still exists nor no longer exists after death.’

segs.p: Evaṁ jānaṁ kho, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako evaṁ passaṁ evaṁ abyākaraṇadhammo hoti abyākatavatthūsu.
segs.e: Knowing and seeing this, a learned noble disciple does not declare the undeclared points.

segs.p: Evaṁ jānaṁ kho, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako evaṁ passaṁ na chambhati, na kampati, na vedhati, na santāsaṁ āpajjati abyākatavatthūsu.
segs.e: Knowing and seeing this, a learned noble disciple doesn’t shake, tremble, quake, or get nervous regarding the undeclared points.

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho, bhikkhu, hetu ayaṁ paccayo yena sutavato ariyasāvakassa vicikicchā nuppajjati abyākatavatthūsū”ti.
segs.e: This is the cause, this is the reason why a learned noble disciple has no doubts regarding the undeclared points.”
Numbered Discourses 7.55
6. The Undeclared Points
Places People Are Reborn

segs.p: “Satta ca, bhikkhave, purisagatiyo desessāmi anupādā ca parinibbānaṁ.
segs.e: “Mendicants, I will teach you seven places people are reborn, and complete extinguishment with no fuel for grasping.

segs.p: Taṁ suṇātha, sādhukaṁ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti.
segs.e: Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṁ.
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” the mendicants replied.
The Buddha said this:
“And what are the seven places people are reborn?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: Take a mendicant who practices like this:

segs.p: ‘no cassa no ca me siyā, na bhavissati na me bhavissati, yadatthi yaṁ bhūtaṁ taṁ pajahāmī’ti upekkhaṁ paṭilabhati.
segs.e: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine. I am giving up what exists, what has come to be.’ They gain equanimity.

segs.p: So bhave na rajjati, sambhave na rajjati, atthuttari padaṁ santaṁ sammappaññāya passati.
segs.e: They’re not attached to life, or to creating a new life. And they see with right wisdom that there is a peaceful state beyond.

segs.p: Tañca khvassa padaṁ na sabbena sabbaṁ sacchikataṁ hoti, tassa na sabbena sabbaṁ mānānusayo pahīno hoti, na sabbena sabbaṁ bhavarāgānusayo pahīno hoti, na sabbena sabbaṁ avijjānusayo pahīno hoti.
segs.e: But they haven’t completely realized that state. They haven’t totally given up the underlying tendencies of conceit, desire for continued existence, and ignorance.

segs.p: So pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā antarāparinibbāyī hoti.
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished between one life and the next.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṁsantatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā nibbāyeyya.
segs.e: Suppose you struck an iron pot that had been heated all day. Any spark that flew off would be extinguished.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant who practices like this …

segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant who practices like this …
‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. …’

segs.p: so pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā upahaccaparinibbāyī hoti.
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished upon landing.

segs.p: Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: Take a mendicant who practices like this:
‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. …’

segs.p: so pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti.
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished without extra effort.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṁsantatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā paritte tiṇapuñje vā kaṭṭhapuñje vā nipateyya.
segs.e: Suppose you struck an iron pot that had been heated all day. Any spark that flew off and floated away would fall on a little heap of grass or twigs.

segs.p: Sā tattha aggimpi janeyya, dhūmampi janeyya, aggimpi janetvā dhūmampi janetvā tameva parittaṁ tiṇapuñjaṁ vā kaṭṭhapuñjaṁ vā pariyādiyitvā anāhārā nibbāyeyya.
segs.e: There it would ignite a fire and produce smoke. But the fire would consume the grass or twigs and become extinguished due to not being fed.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant who practices like this …
‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. …’

segs.p: so pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti.
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished without extra effort.

segs.p: Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: Take a mendicant who practices like this:
‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. …’

segs.p: so pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti.
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished with extra effort.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṁsantatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā vipule tiṇapuñje vā kaṭṭhapuñje vā nipateyya.
segs.e: Suppose you struck an iron pot that had been heated all day. Any spark that flew off and floated away would fall on a large heap of grass or twigs.

segs.p: Sā tattha aggimpi janeyya, dhūmampi janeyya, aggimpi janetvā dhūmampi janetvā tameva vipulaṁ tiṇapuñjaṁ vā kaṭṭhapuñjaṁ vā pariyādiyitvā anāhārā nibbāyeyya.
segs.e: There it would ignite a fire and produce smoke. But the fire would consume the grass or twigs and become extinguished due to not being fed.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant who practices like this …
‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. …’

segs.p: so pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti.
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished with extra effort.

segs.p: Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: Take a mendicant who practices like this:

segs.p: ‘no cassa no ca me siyā, na bhavissati na me bhavissati, yadatthi yaṁ bhūtaṁ taṁ pajahāmī’ti upekkhaṁ paṭilabhati.
segs.e: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine. I am giving up what exists, what has come to be.’ They gain equanimity.

segs.p: So bhave na rajjati, sambhave na rajjati, atthuttari padaṁ santaṁ sammappaññāya passati.
segs.e: They’re not attached to life, or to creating a new life. And they see with right wisdom that there is a peaceful state beyond.

segs.p: Tañca khvassa padaṁ na sabbena sabbaṁ sacchikataṁ hoti, tassa na sabbena sabbaṁ mānānusayo pahīno hoti, na sabbena sabbaṁ bhavarāgānusayo pahīno hoti, na sabbena sabbaṁ avijjānusayo pahīno hoti.
segs.e: But they haven’t totally realized that state. They haven’t completely given up the underlying tendencies of conceit, desire for continued existence, and ignorance.

segs.p: So pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā uddhaṁsoto hoti akaniṭṭhagāmī.
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṁsantatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā mahante tiṇapuñje vā kaṭṭhapuñje vā nipateyya.
segs.e: Suppose you struck an iron pot that had been heated all day. Any spark that flew off and floated away would fall on a big heap of grass or twigs.

segs.p: Sā tattha aggimpi janeyya, dhūmampi janeyya, aggimpi janetvā dhūmampi janetvā tameva mahantaṁ tiṇapuñjaṁ vā kaṭṭhapuñjaṁ vā pariyādiyitvā gacchampi daheyya, dāyampi daheyya, gacchampi dahitvā dāyampi dahitvā haritantaṁ vā pathantaṁ vā selantaṁ vā udakantaṁ vā ramaṇīyaṁ vā bhūmibhāgaṁ āgamma anāhārā nibbāyeyya.
segs.e: There it would ignite a fire and produce smoke. And after consuming the grass and twigs, the fire would burn up plants and trees until it reached a green field, a roadside, a cliff’s edge, a body of water, or cleared parkland, where it would be extinguished due to not being fed.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant who practices like this …
‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. …’

segs.p: so pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā uddhaṁsoto hoti akaniṭṭhagāmī.
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
These are the seven places people are reborn.
And what is complete extinguishment with no fuel for grasping?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṁ paṭipanno hoti:
segs.e: Take a mendicant who practices like this:

segs.p: ‘no cassa no ca me siyā, na bhavissati na me bhavissati, yadatthi yaṁ bhūtaṁ taṁ pajahāmī’ti upekkhaṁ paṭilabhati.
segs.e: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine. It will not be, and it will not be mine. I am giving up what exists, what has come to be.’ They gain equanimity.

segs.p: So bhave na rajjati, sambhave na rajjati, atthuttari padaṁ santaṁ sammappaññāya passati.
segs.e: They’re not attached to life, or to creating a new life. And they see with right wisdom that there is a peaceful state beyond.

segs.p: Tañca khvassa padaṁ sabbena sabbaṁ sacchikataṁ hoti, tassa sabbena sabbaṁ mānānusayo pahīno hoti, sabbena sabbaṁ bhavarāgānusayo pahīno hoti, sabbena sabbaṁ avijjānusayo pahīno hoti.
segs.e: And they have totally realized that state. They’ve completely given up the underlying tendencies of conceit, desire for continued existence, and ignorance.

segs.p: So āsavānaṁ khayā …pe… sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: They’ve realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.
This is called complete extinguishment with no fuel for grasping.

segs.p: Imā kho, bhikkhave, satta purisagatiyo anupādā ca parinibbānan”ti.
segs.e: These are the seven places people are reborn, and complete extinguishment with no fuel for grasping.”
Numbered Discourses 7.56
6. The Undeclared Points
Tissa the Divinity
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

segs.p: Atha kho dve devatā abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇā kevalakappaṁ gijjhakūṭaṁ obhāsetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ aṭṭhaṁsu. Ekamantaṁ ṭhitā kho ekā devatā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then, late at night, two glorious deities, lighting up the entire Vulture’s Peak, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. One deity said to him,
“Sir, these nuns are freed!”
The other deity said to him,
“Sir, these nuns are well freed with no residue!”
This is what those deities said,
and the Teacher concurred.

segs.p: Atha kho tā devatā “samanuñño satthā”ti bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā tatthevantaradhāyiṁsu.
segs.e: Then those deities, knowing that the Teacher concurred, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right, before vanishing right there.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tassā rattiyā accayena bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha told the mendicants all that had happened.

segs.p: “imaṁ, bhikkhave, rattiṁ dve devatā abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇā kevalakappaṁ gijjhakūṭaṁ obhāsetvā yenāhaṁ tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā maṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ aṭṭhaṁsu. Ekamantaṁ ṭhitā kho, bhikkhave, ekā devatā maṁ etadavoca:
Idaṁ vatvā maṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā tatthevantaradhāyiṁsū”ti.
Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato avidūre nisinno hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was sitting not far from the Buddha.
He thought,
“Which gods know whether a person has remainder or not?”

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena tisso nāma bhikkhu adhunākālaṅkato aññataraṁ brahmalokaṁ upapanno hoti.
segs.e: Now, at that time a monk named Tissa had recently passed away and been reborn in a realm of divinity.
There they knew that
Tissa the Divinity was very mighty and powerful.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno—seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṁ vā bāhaṁ pasāreyya, pasāritaṁ vā bāhaṁ samiñjeyya; evamevaṁ—gijjhakūṭe pabbate antarahito tasmiṁ brahmaloke pāturahosi.
segs.e: And then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from the Vulture’s Peak and reappeared in that realm of divinity.

segs.p: Addasā kho tisso brahmā āyasmantaṁ mahāmoggallānaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: Tissa saw Moggallāna coming off in the distance,
and said to him,
“Come, my good Moggallāna!
Welcome, my good Moggallāna!

segs.p: Cirassaṁ kho, mārisa moggallāna, imaṁ pariyāyamakāsi, yadidaṁ idhāgamanāya.
segs.e: It’s been a long time since you took the opportunity to come here.
Sit, my good Moggallāna, here, a seat is ready.”

segs.p: Nisīdi kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno paññatte āsane.
segs.e: Moggallāna sat down on the seat spread out.

segs.p: Tissopi kho brahmā āyasmantaṁ mahāmoggallānaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then Tissa bowed to Moggallāna and sat to one side.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho tissaṁ brahmānaṁ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca:
segs.e: Moggallāna said to him,

segs.p: “katamesānaṁ kho, tissa, devānaṁ evaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: “Which gods know whether a person has remainder or not?”

segs.p: “Brahmakāyikānaṁ kho, mārisa moggallāna, devānaṁ evaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: “The gods of the Divinity’s host know this.”

segs.p: “Sabbesaññeva kho, tissa, brahmakāyikānaṁ devānaṁ evaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: “But do all of them know this?”

segs.p: “Na kho, mārisa moggallāna, sabbesaṁ brahmakāyikānaṁ devānaṁ evaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: “No, my good Moggallāna, not all of them.

segs.p: Ye kho te, mārisa moggallāna, brahmakāyikā devā brahmena āyunā santuṭṭhā brahmena vaṇṇena brahmena sukhena brahmena yasena brahmena ādhipateyyena santuṭṭhā, te uttari nissaraṇaṁ yathābhūtaṁ nappajānanti.
segs.e: Those gods of the Divinity’s host who are content with the lifespan of the Divinity, with the beauty, happiness, glory, and sovereignty of the Divinity, and who don’t truly understand any escape beyond:
they don’t know this.

segs.p: Ye ca kho te, mārisa moggallāna, brahmakāyikā devā brahmena āyunā asantuṭṭhā, brahmena vaṇṇena brahmena sukhena brahmena yasena brahmena ādhipateyyena asantuṭṭhā, te ca uttari nissaraṇaṁ yathābhūtaṁ pajānanti.
segs.e: But those gods of the Divinity’s host who are not content with the lifespan of the Divinity, with the beauty, happiness, glory, and sovereignty of the Divinity, and who do truly understand any escape beyond:
they do know this.

segs.p: Idha, mārisa moggallāna, bhikkhu ubhatobhāgavimutto hoti.
segs.e: Take a mendicant who is freed both ways.
The gods know of them:
‘This venerable is freed both ways.

segs.p: Yāvassa kāyo ṭhassati tāva naṁ dakkhanti devamanussā.
segs.e: As long as their body remains they will be seen by gods and humans.

segs.p: Kāyassa bhedā na naṁ dakkhanti devamanussā’ti.
segs.e: But when their body breaks up gods and humans will see them no more.’

segs.p: Evampi kho, mārisa moggallāna, tesaṁ devānaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: This too is how those gods know whether a person has remainder or not.

segs.p: Idha pana, mārisa moggallāna, bhikkhu paññāvimutto hoti.
segs.e: Take a mendicant who is freed by wisdom.
The gods know of them:
‘This venerable is freed by wisdom.

segs.p: Yāvassa kāyo ṭhassati tāva naṁ dakkhanti devamanussā.
segs.e: As long as their body remains they will be seen by gods and humans.

segs.p: Kāyassa bhedā na naṁ dakkhanti devamanussā’ti.
segs.e: But when their body breaks up gods and humans will see them no more.’

segs.p: Evampi kho, mārisa moggallāna, tesaṁ devānaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: This too is how those gods know whether a person has remainder or not.

segs.p: Idha pana, mārisa moggallāna, bhikkhu kāyasakkhī hoti.
segs.e: Take a mendicant who is a direct witness.
The gods know of them:
‘This venerable is a direct witness.

segs.p: Appeva nāma ayamāyasmā anulomikāni senāsanāni paṭisevamāno kalyāṇamitte bhajamāno indriyāni samannānayamāno—
segs.e: Hopefully this venerable will frequent appropriate lodgings, associate with good friends, and control their faculties.

segs.p: yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṁ—brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti.
segs.e: Then they might realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life, and live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

segs.p: Evampi kho, mārisa moggallāna, tesaṁ devānaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: This too is how those gods know whether a person has remainder or not.

segs.p: Idha pana, mārisa moggallāna, bhikkhu diṭṭhippatto hoti …pe…
segs.e: Take a mendicant who is attained to view. …
freed by faith …
a follower of teachings.
The gods know of them:
‘This venerable is a follower of teachings.

segs.p: Appeva nāma ayamāyasmā anulomikāni senāsanāni paṭisevamāno kalyāṇamitte bhajamāno indriyāni samannānayamāno—
segs.e: Hopefully this venerable will frequent appropriate lodgings, associate with good friends, and control their faculties.

segs.p: yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṁ—brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti.
segs.e: Then they might realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life, and live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

segs.p: Evampi kho, mārisa moggallāna, tesaṁ devānaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: This too is how those gods know whether a person has remainder or not.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno tissassa brahmuno bhāsitaṁ abhinanditvā anumoditvā—seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṁ vā bāhaṁ pasāreyya, pasāritaṁ vā bāhaṁ samiñjeyya; evamevaṁ—brahmaloke antarahito gijjhakūṭe pabbate pāturahosi.
segs.e: Moggallāna approved and agreed with what Tissa the Divinity said. Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared on the Vulture’s Peak.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then Mahāmoggallāna went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno yāvatako ahosi tissena brahmunā saddhiṁ kathāsallāpo taṁ sabbaṁ bhagavato ārocesi.
segs.e: and told him what had happened.

segs.p: “Na hi pana te, moggallāna, tisso brahmā sattamaṁ animittavihāriṁ puggalaṁ deseti”.
segs.e: “But Moggallāna, Tissa the Divinity didn’t teach the seventh individual, the signless meditator.”
“Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One!

segs.p: Yaṁ bhagavā sattamaṁ animittavihāriṁ puggalaṁ deseyya. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti.
segs.e: May the Buddha teach the seventh individual, the signless meditator. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

segs.p: “Tena hi, moggallāna, suṇāhi, sādhukaṁ manasi karohi; bhāsissāmī”ti.
segs.e: “Well then, Moggallāna, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato paccassosi.
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” Mahāmoggallāna replied.
The Buddha said this:

segs.p: “Idha, moggallāna, bhikkhu sabbanimittānaṁ amanasikārā animittaṁ cetosamādhiṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: “Moggallāna, take the case of a mendicant who, not focusing on any signs, enters and remains in the signless immersion of the heart.
The gods know of them:

segs.p: ‘ayaṁ kho āyasmā sabbanimittānaṁ amanasikārā animittaṁ cetosamādhiṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: ‘This venerable, not focusing on any signs, enters and remains in the signless immersion of the heart.

segs.p: Appeva nāma ayamāyasmā anulomikāni senāsanāni paṭisevamāno kalyāṇamitte bhajamāno indriyāni samannānayamāno—
segs.e: Hopefully this venerable will frequent appropriate lodgings, associate with good friends, and control their faculties.

segs.p: yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṁ—brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti.
segs.e: Then they might realize the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life, and live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.’

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, moggallāna, tesaṁ devānaṁ ñāṇaṁ hoti:
segs.e: This too is how those gods know whether a person has remainder or not.”
Numbered Discourses 7.57
6. The Undeclared Points
General Sīha
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā vesāliyaṁ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

segs.p: Atha kho sīho senāpati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho sīho senāpati bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then General Sīha went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “sakkā nu kho, bhante, sandiṭṭhikaṁ dānaphalaṁ paññāpetun”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, can you point out a fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life?”

segs.p: “Tena hi, sīha, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi, yathā te khameyya tathā naṁ byākareyyāsi.
segs.e: “Well then, Sīha, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.
What do you think, Sīha?
Consider two people.

segs.p: eko puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, eko puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato.
segs.e: One is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive. One is a faithful donor who loves charity.

segs.p: Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, sīha, kaṁ nu kho arahanto paṭhamaṁ anukampantā anukampeyyuṁ:
segs.e: Which do you think the perfected ones will show sympathy for first?”

segs.p: ‘yo vā so puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, yo vā so puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato’”ti?
“Yo so, bhante, puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, kintaṁ arahanto paṭhamaṁ anukampantā anukampissanti.
segs.e: “Why would the perfected ones first show sympathy for the person who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive?

segs.p: Yo ca kho so, bhante, puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato taṁyeva arahanto paṭhamaṁ anukampantā anukampeyyuṁ”.
segs.e: They’d show sympathy first for the faithful donor who loves charity.”

segs.p: “Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, sīha, kaṁ nu kho arahanto paṭhamaṁ upasaṅkamantā upasaṅkameyyuṁ:
segs.e: “Which do you think the perfected ones will first approach?”

segs.p: ‘yo vā so puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, yo vā so puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato’”ti?
“Yo so, bhante, puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, kintaṁ arahanto paṭhamaṁ upasaṅkamantā upasaṅkamissanti.
Yo ca kho so, bhante, puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato taṁyeva arahanto paṭhamaṁ upasaṅkamantā upasaṅkameyyuṁ”.
segs.e: “They’d first approach the faithful donor who loves charity.”

segs.p: “Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, sīha, kassa nu kho arahanto paṭhamaṁ paṭiggaṇhantā paṭiggaṇheyyuṁ:
segs.e: “Which do you think the perfected ones will receive alms from first?”

segs.p: ‘yo vā so puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, yo vā so puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato’”ti?
“Yo so, bhante, puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, kintaṁ tassa arahanto paṭhamaṁ paṭiggaṇhantā paṭiggaṇhissanti.
Yo ca kho so, bhante, puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato tasseva arahanto paṭhamaṁ paṭiggaṇhantā paṭiggaṇheyyuṁ”.
segs.e: “They’d receive alms first from the faithful donor who loves charity.”

segs.p: “Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, sīha, kassa nu kho arahanto paṭhamaṁ dhammaṁ desentā deseyyuṁ:
segs.e: “Which do you think the perfected ones will teach the Dhamma to first?”

segs.p: ‘yo vā so puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, yo vā so puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato’”ti?
“Yo so, bhante, puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, kintaṁ tassa arahanto paṭhamaṁ dhammaṁ desentā desessanti.
Yo ca kho so, bhante, puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato tasseva arahanto paṭhamaṁ dhammaṁ desentā deseyyuṁ”.
segs.e: “They’d first teach the Dhamma to the faithful donor who loves charity.”

segs.p: “Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, sīha, kassa nu kho kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggaccheyya:
segs.e: “Which do you think would get a good reputation?”

segs.p: ‘yo vā so puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, yo vā so puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato’”ti?
“Yo so, bhante, puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, kintaṁ tassa kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchissati.
Yo ca kho so, bhante, puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato tasseva kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggaccheyya”.
segs.e: “The faithful donor who loves charity would get a good reputation.”

segs.p: “Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, sīha, ko nu kho yaṁyadeva parisaṁ upasaṅkameyya, yadi khattiyaparisaṁ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṁ yadi gahapatiparisaṁ yadi samaṇaparisaṁ visārado upasaṅkameyya amaṅkubhūto:
segs.e: “Which do you think would enter any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics?”

segs.p: ‘yo vā so puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, yo vā so puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato’”ti?

“Yo so, bhante, puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, kiṁ so yaṁyadeva parisaṁ upasaṅkamissati, yadi khattiyaparisaṁ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṁ yadi gahapatiparisaṁ yadi samaṇaparisaṁ visārado upasaṅkamissati amaṅkubhūto.
segs.e: “How could the person who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive enter any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics?

segs.p: Yo ca kho so, bhante, puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato so yaṁyadeva parisaṁ upasaṅkameyya, yadi khattiyaparisaṁ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṁ yadi gahapatiparisaṁ yadi samaṇaparisaṁ visārado upasaṅkameyya amaṅkubhūto”.
segs.e: The faithful donor who loves charity would enter any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.”

segs.p: “Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, sīha, ko nu kho kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjeyya:
segs.e: “When their body breaks up, after death, which do you think would be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm?”

segs.p: ‘yo vā so puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, yo vā so puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato’”ti?
“Yo so, bhante, puriso assaddho maccharī kadariyo paribhāsako, kiṁ so kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjissati.
segs.e: “Why would the person who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm?

segs.p: Yo ca kho so, bhante, puriso saddho dānapati anuppadānarato so kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjeyya.
segs.e: The faithful donor who loves charity would, when their body breaks up, after death, be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Yānimāni, bhante, bhagavatā sandiṭṭhikāni dānaphalāni akkhātāni, nāhaṁ ettha bhagavato saddhāya gacchāmi.
segs.e: When it comes to these fruits of giving that are apparent in the present life, I don’t rely on faith in the Buddha,
for I know them too.

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati, maṁ arahanto paṭhamaṁ anukampantā anukampanti.
segs.e: I’m a giver, a donor, and the perfected ones show sympathy for me first.

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati, maṁ arahanto paṭhamaṁ upasaṅkamantā upasaṅkamanti.
segs.e: I’m a giver, and the perfected ones approach me first.

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati, mayhaṁ arahanto paṭhamaṁ paṭiggaṇhantā paṭiggaṇhanti.
segs.e: I’m a giver, and the perfected ones receive alms from me first.

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati, mayhaṁ arahanto paṭhamaṁ dhammaṁ desentā desenti.
segs.e: I’m a giver, and the perfected ones teach me Dhamma first.

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati, mayhaṁ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato:
segs.e: I’m a giver, and I have this good reputation:
‘General Sīha gives, serves, and attends on the Saṅgha.’

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati yaṁyadeva parisaṁ upasaṅkamāmi, yadi khattiyaparisaṁ …pe… yadi samaṇaparisaṁ visārado upasaṅkamāmi amaṅkubhūto.
segs.e: I’m a giver, I enter any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

segs.p: Yānimāni, bhante, bhagavatā sandiṭṭhikāni dānaphalāni akkhātāni, nāhaṁ ettha bhagavato saddhāya gacchāmi.
segs.e: When it comes to these fruits of giving that are apparent in the present life, I don’t rely on faith in the Buddha,
for I know them too.

segs.p: Yañca kho maṁ, bhante, bhagavā evamāha:
segs.e: But when the Buddha says:

segs.p: ‘dāyako, sīha, dānapati kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘When a giver’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ I don’t know this,

segs.p: Etāhaṁ na jānāmi, ettha ca panāhaṁ, bhagavato saddhāya gacchāmī”ti.
segs.e: so I rely on faith in the Buddha.”
“That’s so true, Sīha! That’s so true!

segs.p: Dāyako, sīha, dānapati kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjatī”ti.
segs.e: When a giver’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.”
Numbered Discourses 7.58
6. The Undeclared Points
Nothing to Hide

segs.p: “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāgatassa arakkheyyāni, tīhi ca anupavajjo.
segs.e: “Mendicants, there are four areas where the Realized One has nothing to hide, and three ways he is irreproachable.
What are the four areas where the Realized One has nothing to hide?
His bodily behavior is pure.

segs.p: natthi tathāgatassa kāyaduccaritaṁ yaṁ tathāgato rakkheyya:
segs.e: So the Realized One has no bodily misconduct to hide, thinking:
‘Don’t let others find this out about me!’
His verbal behavior is pure.

segs.p: natthi tathāgatassa vacīduccaritaṁ yaṁ tathāgato rakkheyya:
segs.e: So the Realized One has no verbal misconduct to hide, thinking:
‘Don’t let others find this out about me!’
His mental behavior is pure.

segs.p: natthi tathāgatassa manoduccaritaṁ yaṁ tathāgato rakkheyya:
segs.e: So the Realized One has no mental misconduct to hide, thinking:
‘Don’t let others find this out about me!’
His livelihood is pure.

segs.p: natthi tathāgatassa micchāājīvo yaṁ tathāgato rakkheyya:
segs.e: So the Realized One has no wrong livelihood to hide, thinking:
‘Don’t let others find this out about me!’
These are the four areas where the Realized One has nothing to hide.
What are the three ways the Realized One is irreproachable?
The Realized One has explained the teaching well.

segs.p: Tatra vata maṁ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṁ sahadhammena paṭicodessati:
segs.e: I see no reason for anyone—whether ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or the Divinity, or anyone else in the world—to legitimately scold me, saying:
‘For such reasons you haven’t explained the teaching well.’

segs.p: Etamahaṁ, bhikkhave, nimittaṁ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.
segs.e: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.

segs.p: Supaññattā kho pana me, bhikkhave, sāvakānaṁ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā.
segs.e: I have clearly described the practice that leads to extinguishment for my disciples.

segs.p: Yathāpaṭipannā mama sāvakā āsavānaṁ khayā anāsavaṁ cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti.
segs.e: Practicing in accordance with this, my disciples realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Tatra vata maṁ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṁ sahadhammena paṭicodessati:
segs.e: I see no reason for anyone—whether ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or the Divinity, or anyone else in the world—to legitimately scold me, saying:

segs.p: ‘itipi te na supaññattā sāvakānaṁ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā. Yathāpaṭipannā tava sāvakā āsavānaṁ khayā …pe… sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī’ti.
segs.e: ‘For such reasons you haven’t clearly described the practice that leads to extinguishment for your disciples.’

segs.p: Etamahaṁ, bhikkhave, nimittaṁ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.
segs.e: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.

segs.p: Anekasatā kho pana me, bhikkhave, sāvakaparisā āsavānaṁ khayā …pe… sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti.
segs.e: Many hundreds in my assembly of disciples have realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Tatra vata maṁ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṁ sahadhammena paṭicodessati:
segs.e: I see no reason for anyone—whether ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or the Divinity, or anyone else in the world—to legitimately scold me, saying:

segs.p: ‘itipi te na anekasatā sāvakaparisā āsavānaṁ khayā anāsavaṁ cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī’ti.
segs.e: ‘For such reasons you don’t have many hundreds of disciples in your following who have realized the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and who live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.’

segs.p: Etamahaṁ, bhikkhave, nimittaṁ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.
segs.e: Since I see no such reason, I live secure, fearless, and self-assured.
These are the three ways the Realized One is irreproachable.

segs.p: Imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri tathāgatassa arakkheyyāni, imehi ca tīhi anupavajjo”ti.
segs.e: These are the four areas where the Realized One has nothing to hide, and the three ways he is irreproachable.”
Numbered Discourses 7.59
6. The Undeclared Points
With Kimbila
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā kimilāyaṁ viharati niculavane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kimbilā in the Freshwater Mangrove Wood.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā kimilo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā kimilo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Kimbila went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo yena tathāgate parinibbute saddhammo na ciraṭṭhitiko hotī”ti?
segs.e: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why the true teaching does not last long after the final quenching of the Realized One?”

segs.p: “Idha, kimila, tathāgate parinibbute bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo satthari agāravā viharanti appatissā, dhamme agāravā viharanti appatissā, saṅghe agāravā viharanti appatissā, sikkhāya agāravā viharanti appatissā, samādhismiṁ agāravā viharanti appatissā, appamāde agāravā viharanti appatissā, paṭisanthāre agāravā viharanti appatissā.
segs.e: “Kimbila, it’s when the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen lack respect and reverence for the Teacher, the teaching, the Saṅgha, the training, immersion, diligence, and hospitality after the final quenching of the Realized One.

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho, kimila, hetu ayaṁ paccayo yena tathāgate parinibbute saddhammo na ciraṭṭhitiko hotī”ti.
segs.e: This is the cause, this is the reason why the true teaching does not last long after the final quenching of the Realized One.”

segs.p: “Ko pana, bhante, hetu ko paccayo yena tathāgate parinibbute saddhammo ciraṭṭhitiko hotī”ti?
segs.e: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why the true teaching does last long after the final quenching of the Realized One?”

segs.p: “Idha, kimila, tathāgate parinibbute bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo satthari sagāravā viharanti sappatissā, dhamme sagāravā viharanti sappatissā, saṅghe sagāravā viharanti sappatissā, sikkhāya sagāravā viharanti sappatissā, samādhismiṁ sagāravā viharanti sappatissā, appamāde sagāravā viharanti sappatissā, paṭisanthāre sagāravā viharanti sappatissā.
segs.e: “Kimbila, it’s when the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen maintain respect and reverence for the Teacher, the teaching, the Saṅgha, the training, immersion, diligence, and hospitality after the final quenching of the Realized One.

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho, kimila, hetu ayaṁ paccayo yena tathāgate parinibbute saddhammo ciraṭṭhitiko hotī”ti.
segs.e: This is the cause, this is the reason why the true teaching does last long after the final quenching of the Realized One.”
Numbered Discourses 7.60
6. The Undeclared Points
Seven Qualities

segs.p: “Sattahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu nacirasseva āsavānaṁ khayā …pe… sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyya.
segs.e: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities soon realizes the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.
What seven?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saddho hoti, sīlavā hoti, bahussuto hoti, paṭisallīno hoti, āraddhavīriyo hoti, satimā hoti, paññavā hoti.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant is faithful, ethical, learned, secluded, energetic, mindful, and wise.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, sattahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu nacirasseva āsavānaṁ khayā …pe… sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā”ti.
segs.e: A mendicant with these seven qualities soon realizes the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They live having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.”
Numbered Discourses 7.61
6. The Undeclared Points
Nodding Off
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā bhaggesu viharati susumāragire bhesakaḷāvane migadāye.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Bhaggas at Crocodile’s Bellow, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā’s Wood.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahāmoggallāno magadhesu kallavāḷaputtagāme pacalāyamāno nisinno hoti.
segs.e: Now at that time, in the land of the Magadhans near Kallavāḷamutta Village, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was nodding off while meditating.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena āyasmantaṁ mahāmoggallānaṁ magadhesu kallavāḷaputtagāme pacalāyamānaṁ nisinnaṁ.
segs.e: The Buddha saw him with his clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman.

segs.p: seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṁ vā bāhaṁ pasāreyya, pasāritaṁ vā bāhaṁ samiñjeyya; evamevaṁ—bhaggesu susumāragire bhesakaḷāvane migadāye antarahito magadhesu kallavāḷaputtagāme āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa sammukhe pāturahosi.
segs.e: Then, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the deer park at Bhesakaḷā’s Wood in the land of the Bhaggas and reappeared in front of Mahāmoggallāna near Kallavāḷamutta Village in the land of the Magadhans.
He sat down on the seat spread out

segs.p: Nisajja kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ mahāmoggallānaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: and said to Mahāmoggallāna,

segs.p: “Pacalāyasi no tvaṁ, moggallāna, pacalāyasi no tvaṁ, moggallānā”ti?
segs.e: “Are you nodding off, Moggallāna? Are you nodding off?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Tasmātiha, moggallāna, yathāsaññissa te viharato taṁ middhaṁ okkamati, taṁ saññaṁ mā manasākāsi, taṁ saññaṁ mā bahulamakāsi.
segs.e: “So, Moggallāna, don’t focus on or cultivate the perception that you were meditating on when you fell drowsy.

segs.p: Ṭhānaṁ kho panetaṁ, moggallāna, vijjati yaṁ te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha.
segs.e: It’s possible that you’ll give up drowsiness in this way.

segs.p: No ce te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha, tato tvaṁ, moggallāna, yathāsutaṁ yathāpariyattaṁ dhammaṁ cetasā anuvitakkeyyāsi anuvicāreyyāsi, manasā anupekkheyyāsi.
segs.e: But what if that doesn’t work? Then think about and consider the teaching as you’ve learned and memorized it, examining it with your mind.

segs.p: Ṭhānaṁ kho panetaṁ vijjati yaṁ te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha.
segs.e: It’s possible that you’ll give up drowsiness in this way.

segs.p: No ce te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha, tato tvaṁ, moggallāna, yathāsutaṁ yathāpariyattaṁ dhammaṁ vitthārena sajjhāyaṁ kareyyāsi.
segs.e: But what if that doesn’t work? Then rehearse in detail the teaching as you’ve learned and memorized it.

segs.p: Ṭhānaṁ kho panetaṁ vijjati yaṁ te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha.
segs.e: It’s possible that you’ll give up drowsiness in this way.

segs.p: No ce te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha, tato tvaṁ, moggallāna, ubho kaṇṇasotāni āviñcheyyāsi, pāṇinā gattāni anumajjeyyāsi.
segs.e: But what if that doesn’t work? Then pinch your ears and rub your limbs.

segs.p: Ṭhānaṁ kho panetaṁ vijjati yaṁ te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha.
segs.e: It’s possible that you’ll give up drowsiness in this way.

segs.p: No ce te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha, tato tvaṁ, moggallāna, uṭṭhāyāsanā udakena akkhīni anumajjitvā disā anuvilokeyyāsi, nakkhattāni tārakarūpāni ullokeyyāsi.
segs.e: But what if that doesn’t work? Then get up from your seat, flush your eyes with water, look around in every direction, and look up at the stars and constellations.

segs.p: Ṭhānaṁ kho panetaṁ vijjati yaṁ te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha.
segs.e: It’s possible that you’ll give up drowsiness in this way.

segs.p: No ce te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha, tato tvaṁ, moggallāna, ālokasaññaṁ manasi kareyyāsi, divāsaññaṁ adhiṭṭhaheyyāsi—
segs.e: But what if that doesn’t work? Then apply your mind to the perception of light, focusing on the perception of day:

segs.p: yathā divā tathā rattiṁ yathā rattiṁ tathā divā.
segs.e: as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.

segs.p: Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṁ cittaṁ bhāveyyāsi.
segs.e: And so, with an open and unenveloped heart, develop a mind that’s full of radiance.

segs.p: Ṭhānaṁ kho panetaṁ vijjati yaṁ te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha.
segs.e: It’s possible that you’ll give up drowsiness in this way.

segs.p: No ce te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha, tato tvaṁ, moggallāna, pacchāpuresaññī caṅkamaṁ adhiṭṭhaheyyāsi antogatehi indriyehi abahigatena mānasena.
segs.e: But what if that doesn’t work? Then walk mindfully, focusing on the perception of before and behind, your faculties directed inwards and your mind not scattered outside.

segs.p: Ṭhānaṁ kho panetaṁ vijjati yaṁ te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha.
segs.e: It’s possible that you’ll give up drowsiness in this way.

segs.p: No ce te evaṁ viharato taṁ middhaṁ pahīyetha, tato tvaṁ, moggallāna, dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṁ kappeyyāsi pāde pādaṁ accādhāya sato sampajāno uṭṭhānasaññaṁ manasi karitvā.
segs.e: But what if that doesn’t work? Then lie down in the lion’s posture—on the right side, placing one foot on top of the other—mindful and aware, and focused on the time of getting up.

segs.p: Paṭibuddhena ca te, moggallāna, khippaññeva paccuṭṭhātabbaṁ:
segs.e: When you wake, you should get up quickly, thinking:

segs.p: ‘na seyyasukhaṁ na passasukhaṁ na middhasukhaṁ anuyutto viharissāmī’ti.
segs.e: ‘I will not live indulging in the pleasures of sleeping, lying down, and drowsing.’
That’s how you should train.
So you should train like this:
‘I will not approach families with my head swollen with vanity.’
That’s how you should train.

segs.p: Sace, moggallāna, bhikkhu uccāsoṇḍaṁ paggahetvā kulāni upasaṅkamati, santi hi, moggallāna, kulesu kiccakaraṇīyāni.
segs.e: What happens if a mendicant approaches families with a head swollen with vanity? Well, families have business to attend to,

segs.p: Yehi manussā āgataṁ bhikkhuṁ na manasi karonti, tatra bhikkhussa evaṁ hoti:
segs.e: so people might not notice when a mendicant arrives. In that case the mendicant thinks:

segs.p: ‘kosu nāma idāni maṁ imasmiṁ kule paribhindi, virattarūpā dānime mayi manussā’ti.
segs.e: ‘Who on earth has turned this family against me? It seems they don’t like me any more.’

segs.p: Itissa alābhena maṅkubhāvo, maṅkubhūtassa uddhaccaṁ, uddhatassa asaṁvaro, asaṁvutassa ārā cittaṁ samādhimhā.
segs.e: And so, because they don’t get anything they feel dismayed. Being dismayed, they become restless. Being restless, they lose restraint. And without restraint the mind is far from immersion.
So you should train like this:
‘I won’t get into arguments.’
That’s how you should train.

segs.p: Viggāhikāya, moggallāna, kathāya sati kathābāhullaṁ pāṭikaṅkhaṁ, kathābāhulle sati uddhaccaṁ, uddhatassa asaṁvaro, asaṁvutassa ārā cittaṁ samādhimhā.
segs.e: When there’s an argument, you can expect there’ll be lots of talking. When there’s lots of talking, people become restless. Being restless, they lose restraint. And without restraint the mind is far from immersion.
Moggallāna, I don’t praise all kinds of closeness.

segs.p: Na panāhaṁ, moggallāna, sabbeheva saṁsaggaṁ na vaṇṇayāmi.
segs.e: Nor do I criticize all kinds of closeness.

segs.p: Sagahaṭṭhapabbajitehi kho ahaṁ, moggallāna, saṁsaggaṁ na vaṇṇayāmi.
segs.e: I don’t praise closeness with laypeople and renunciates.

segs.p: Yāni ca kho tāni senāsanāni appasaddāni appanigghosāni vijanavātāni manussarāhasseyyakāni paṭisallānasāruppāni tathārūpehi senāsanehi saṁsaggaṁ vaṇṇayāmī”ti.
segs.e: I do praise closeness with those lodgings that are quiet and still, far from the madding crowd, remote from human settlements, and fit for retreat.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he said this, Venerable Moggallāna asked the Buddha,

segs.p: “kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, bhikkhu saṅkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti accantaniṭṭho accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosāno seṭṭho devamanussānan”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, how do you briefly define a mendicant who is freed through the ending of craving, who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal, and is best among gods and humans?”
“Take a mendicant who has heard:
‘Nothing is worth insisting on.’
When a mendicant has heard that
nothing is worth insisting on,

segs.p: So sabbaṁ dhammaṁ abhijānāti, sabbaṁ dhammaṁ abhiññāya sabbaṁ dhammaṁ parijānāti. Sabbaṁ dhammaṁ pariññāya yaṁ kiñci vedanaṁ vediyati sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā.
segs.e: they directly know all things. Directly knowing all things, they completely understand all things. Completely understanding all things, when they experience any kind of feeling—pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral—

segs.p: So tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati.
segs.e: they meditate observing impermanence, dispassion, cessation, and letting go in those feelings.

segs.p: So tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharanto virāgānupassī viharanto nirodhānupassī viharanto paṭinissaggānupassī viharanto na kiñci loke upādiyati,
segs.e: Meditating in this way, they don’t grasp at anything in the world.

segs.p: anupādiyaṁ na paritassati, aparitassaṁ paccattaṁyeva parinibbāyati.
segs.e: Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished.

segs.p: ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, kataṁ karaṇīyaṁ, nāparaṁ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

segs.p: Ettāvatā kho, moggallāna, bhikkhu saṅkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti accantaniṭṭho accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosāno seṭṭho devamanussānan”ti.
segs.e: That’s how I briefly define a mendicant who is freed through the ending of craving, who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate sanctuary from the yoke, the ultimate spiritual life, the ultimate goal, and is best among gods and humans.”
Numbered Discourses 7.62
6. The Undeclared Points
Don’t Fear Good Deeds
“Mendicants, don’t fear good deeds.
For ‘good deeds’ is a term for happiness.

segs.p: Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṁ, bhikkhave, dīgharattaṁ katānaṁ puññānaṁ dīgharattaṁ iṭṭhaṁ kantaṁ manāpaṁ vipākaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ.
segs.e: I recall undergoing for a long time the likable, desirable, and agreeable results of good deeds performed over a long time.
I developed a mind of love for seven years.

segs.p: Satta vassāni mettacittaṁ bhāvetvā satta saṁvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe nayimaṁ lokaṁ punāgamāsiṁ.
segs.e: As a result, for seven eons of the cosmos contracting and expanding I didn’t return to this world again.

segs.p: Saṁvaṭṭamāne sudāhaṁ, bhikkhave, loke ābhassarūpago homi,
segs.e: As the cosmos contracted I went to the realm of sublime luminosity.
As it expanded I was reborn in an empty mansion of divinity.

segs.p: Tatra sudaṁ, bhikkhave, brahmā homi mahābrahmā abhibhū anabhibhūto aññadatthudaso vasavattī.
segs.e: There I was the Divinity, the Great Divinity, the vanquisher, the unvanquished, the universal seer, the wielder of power.

segs.p: Chattiṁsakkhattuṁ kho panāhaṁ, bhikkhave, sakko ahosiṁ devānamindo;
segs.e: I was Sakka, lord of gods, thirty-six times.

segs.p: anekasatakkhattuṁ rājā ahosiṁ cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato.
segs.e: Many hundreds of times I was a king, a wheel-turning monarch, a just and principled king. My dominion extended to all four sides, I achieved stability in the country, and I possessed the seven treasures.

segs.p: Tassa mayhaṁ, bhikkhave, imāni satta ratanāni ahesuṁ, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: These were my seven treasures:

segs.p: cakkaratanaṁ, hatthiratanaṁ, assaratanaṁ, maṇiratanaṁ, itthiratanaṁ, gahapatiratanaṁ, pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṁ.
segs.e: the wheel, the elephant, the horse, the jewel, the woman, the householder, and the commander as the seventh treasure.

segs.p: Parosahassaṁ kho pana me, bhikkhave, puttā ahesuṁ sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā.
segs.e: I had over a thousand sons who were valiant and heroic, crushing the armies of my enemies.

segs.p: So imaṁ pathaviṁ sāgarapariyantaṁ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasinti.
segs.e: After conquering this land girt by sea, I reigned by principle, without rod or sword.
See the result of good deeds,
of skillful deeds, for one seeking happiness.
I developed a mind of love
for seven years, mendicants.
For seven eons of expansion and contraction
I didn’t return to this world again.
As the world contracted
I went to the realm of sublime luminosity.
And when it expanded
I went to an empty mansion of divinity.
Seven times I was a Great Divinity,
and at that time I was the wielder of power.
Thirty-six times I was lord of gods,
acting as ruler of the gods.
Then I was king, a wheel-turning monarch,
lord of the Black Plum Tree Land.
An anointed aristocrat,
I was sovereign of all humans.
Without rod or sword,
I conquered this land.
Through non-violent action
I guided it justly.
After ruling this vast territory
by means of principle,
I was born in a rich family,
affluent and wealthy.
It was replete with all sense pleasures,
and the seven treasures.
This was well taught by the Buddhas,
who bring the world together.
This is the cause of greatness
by which one is called a lord of the land.
I was a majestic king,
with lots of property and assets;
successful and glorious,
lord of the Black Plum Tree Land.
Who would not be inspired by this,
even someone of dark birth.
Therefore someone who desires self-knowledge,
and aspires to greatness themselves,
should respect the true teaching,
remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.”
Numbered Discourses 7.63
6. The Undeclared Points
Kinds of Wives

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa nivesanaṁ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatissa nivesane manussā uccāsaddā mahāsaddā honti.
segs.e: Now at that time people in Anāthapiṇḍika’s home were making a colossal racket.

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho anāthapiṇḍikaṁ gahapatiṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

segs.p: “Kiṁ nu te, gahapati, nivesane manussā uccāsaddā mahāsaddā kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilope”ti?
segs.e: “Householder, what’s with the people making that colossal racket in your home? You’d think it was fishermen hauling in a catch!”
“Sir, that’s my daughter-in-law Sujātā. She’s been brought here from a wealthy family.

segs.p: Sā neva sassuṁ ādiyati, na sasuraṁ ādiyati, na sāmikaṁ ādiyati, bhagavantampi na sakkaroti na garuṁ karoti na māneti na pūjetī”ti.
segs.e: She doesn’t obey her mother-in-law or father-in-law or her husband. And she does not honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Buddha.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sujātaṁ gharasuṇhaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha addressed Sujātā, saying,
“Come, Sujātā.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho sujātā gharasuṇhā bhagavato paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho sujātaṁ gharasuṇhaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” she replied. She went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to her:
“Sujātā, a man can have seven kinds of wife.
What seven?

segs.p: Vadhakasamā, corīsamā, ayyasamā, mātāsamā, bhaginīsamā, sakhīsamā, dāsīsamā.
segs.e: A wife like a killer, a wife like a thief, a wife like a lord, a wife like a mother, a wife like a sister, a wife like a comrade, and a wife like a bondservant.

segs.p: Imā kho, sujāte, satta purisassa bhariyāyo.
segs.e: These are the kinds of wife that a man can have.
Which one of these are you?”

segs.p: “Na kho ahaṁ, bhante, imassa bhagavatā saṅkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṁ ājānāmi.
segs.e: “Sir, I don’t understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha has said in brief.

segs.p: Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā tathā dhammaṁ desetu yathāhaṁ imassa bhagavatā saṅkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṁ jāneyyan”ti.
segs.e: Please teach me this matter so I can understand the detailed meaning.”

segs.p: “Tena hi, sujāte, suṇāhi, sādhukaṁ manasi karohi; bhāsissāmī”ti.
segs.e: “Well then, Sujātā, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho sujātā gharasuṇhā bhagavato paccassosi.
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” she replied.
The Buddha said this:
“With a mind full of hate and no kindness,
lusting for others, looking down on her husband,
she longs to murder him who paid the price for her.
A man’s wife of this sort
is called a wife and a killer.
A woman’s husband earns his wealth
by focusing on a profession, trade, or farming.
And even if it’s only a little, she wants to take it.
A man’s wife of this sort
is called a wife and a thief.
She’s an idle glutton who doesn’t want to work.
Her words are harsh, fierce, and rude.
He works hard, but she lives as his master.
A man’s wife of this sort
is called a wife and a lord.
She’s always caring and kind,
looking after her husband like a mother her child.
She keeps the wealth that he has earned secure.
A man’s wife of this sort
is called a wife and a mother.
She respects her husband
as a younger sister respects her elder.
Conscientious, she does what her husband says.
A man’s wife of this sort
is called a wife and a sister.
She’s delighted to see him,
like one reunited with a long-lost comrade.
She’s of good pedigree, virtuous, and devoted.
A man’s wife of this sort
is called a wife and a comrade.
She has no anger <j>when threatened with violence by the rod.
Without hate or anger,
she endures her husband and does what he says.
A man’s wife of this sort
is called a wife and a bondservant.
The kinds of wives here called
killer, thief, and lord;
immoral, harsh, and lacking regard for others,
when their body breaks up they set course for hell.
But the kinds of wives here called
mother, sister, comrade, and bondservant;
steadfast in their own morality, <j>restrained for a long time,
when their body breaks up <j>they set course for a good place.

segs.p: Imā kho, sujāte, satta purisassa bhariyāyo.
segs.e: Sujātā, these are the seven kinds of wife that a man can have.
Which one of these are you?”

segs.p: “Ajjatagge maṁ, bhante, bhagavā dāsīsamaṁ sāmikassa bhariyaṁ dhāretū”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, from this day forth may the Buddha remember me as a wife like a bondservant.”
Numbered Discourses 7.64
6. The Undeclared Points
Irritable

segs.p: “Sattime, bhikkhave, dhammā sapattakantā sapattakaraṇā kodhanaṁ āgacchanti itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā.
segs.e: “Mendicants, these seven things that please and assist an enemy happen to an irritable woman or man.
What seven?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṁ icchati:
segs.e: Firstly, an enemy wishes for an enemy:
‘If only they’d become ugly!’
Why is that?

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa vaṇṇavatāya nandati.
segs.e: Because an enemy doesn’t like to have a beautiful enemy.

segs.p: Kodhanoyaṁ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto, kiñcāpi so hoti sunhāto suvilitto kappitakesamassu odātavatthavasano;
segs.e: An irritable individual, overcome and overwhelmed by anger, is ugly, even though they’re nicely bathed and anointed, with hair and beard dressed, and wearing white clothes.

segs.p: atha kho so dubbaṇṇova hoti kodhābhibhūto.
Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, paṭhamo dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṁ āgacchati itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā.
segs.e: This is the first thing that pleases and assists an enemy which happens to an irritable woman or man.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṁ icchati:
segs.e: Furthermore, an enemy wishes for an enemy:
‘If only they’d sleep badly!’
Why is that?

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa sukhaseyyāya nandati.
segs.e: Because an enemy doesn’t like to have an enemy who sleeps at ease.

segs.p: Kodhanoyaṁ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto, kiñcāpi so pallaṅke seti gonakatthate paṭalikatthate kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇe sauttaracchade ubhatolohitakūpadhāne;
segs.e: An irritable individual, overcome and overwhelmed by anger, sleeps badly, even though they sleep on a couch spread with woolen covers—shag-piled, pure white, or embroidered with flowers—and spread with a fine deer hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends.

segs.p: atha kho so dukkhaññeva seti kodhābhibhūto.
Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, dutiyo dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṁ āgacchati itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā.
segs.e: This is the second thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṁ icchati:
segs.e: Furthermore, an enemy wishes for an enemy:
‘If only their needs are not amply satisfied!’
Why is that?

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa pacuratthatāya nandati.
segs.e: Because an enemy doesn’t like to have an enemy whose needs are amply satisfied.

segs.p: Kodhanoyaṁ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto, anatthampi gahetvā ‘attho me gahito’ti maññati, atthampi gahetvā ‘anattho me gahito’ti maññati.
segs.e: When an irritable individual, overcome and overwhelmed by anger, gets what they don’t need they think, ‘I’ve got what I need.’ When they get what they need they think, ‘I’ve got what I don’t need.’

segs.p: Tassime dhammā aññamaññaṁ vipaccanīkā gahitā dīgharattaṁ ahitāya dukkhāya saṁvattanti kodhābhibhūtassa.
segs.e: When an angry person gets these things that are the exact opposite of what they need, it’s for their lasting harm and suffering.

segs.p: Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, tatiyo dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṁ āgacchati itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā.
segs.e: This is the third thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṁ icchati:
segs.e: Furthermore, an enemy wishes for an enemy:
‘If only they weren’t wealthy!’
Why is that?

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa bhogavatāya nandati.
segs.e: Because an enemy doesn’t like to have an enemy who is wealthy.

segs.p: Kodhanassa, bhikkhave, purisapuggalassa kodhābhibhūtassa kodhaparetassa, yepissa te honti bhogā uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatā bāhābalaparicitā sedāvakkhittā dhammikā dhammaladdhā, tepi rājāno rājakosaṁ pavesenti kodhābhibhūtassa.
segs.e: When an individual is irritable, overcome and overwhelmed by anger, the rulers seize the legitimate wealth they’ve earned by their efforts, built up with their own hands, gathered by the sweat of their brow.

segs.p: Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, catuttho dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṁ āgacchati itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā.
segs.e: This is the fourth thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṁ icchati:
segs.e: Furthermore, an enemy wishes for an enemy:
‘If only they weren’t famous!’
Why is that?

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa yasavatāya nandati.
segs.e: Because an enemy doesn’t like to have a famous enemy.

segs.p: Kodhanoyaṁ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto, yopissa so hoti yaso appamādādhigato, tamhāpi dhaṁsati kodhābhibhūto.
segs.e: When an individual is irritable, overcome and overwhelmed by anger, any fame they have acquired by diligence falls to dust.

segs.p: Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, pañcamo dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṁ āgacchati itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā.
segs.e: This is the fifth thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṁ icchati:
segs.e: Furthermore, an enemy wishes for an enemy:
‘If only they had no friends!’
Why is that?

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa mittavatāya nandati.
segs.e: Because an enemy doesn’t like to have an enemy with friends.

segs.p: Kodhanaṁ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalaṁ kodhābhibhūtaṁ kodhaparetaṁ, yepissa te honti mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā, tepi ārakā parivajjanti kodhābhibhūtaṁ.
segs.e: When an individual is irritable, overcome and overwhelmed by anger, their friends and colleagues, relatives and kin avoid them from afar.

segs.p: Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, chaṭṭho dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṁ āgacchati itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā.
segs.e: This is the sixth thing …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṁ icchati:
segs.e: Furthermore, an enemy wishes for an enemy:

segs.p: ‘aho vatāyaṁ kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjeyyā’ti.
segs.e: ‘If only, when their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell!’
Why is that?

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa sugatigamane nandati.
segs.e: Because an enemy doesn’t like to have an enemy who goes to a good place.

segs.p: Kodhanoyaṁ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto kāyena duccaritaṁ carati, vācāya duccaritaṁ carati, manasā duccaritaṁ carati.
segs.e: When an individual is irritable, overcome and overwhelmed by anger, they do bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjati kodhābhibhūto.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, sattamo dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṁ āgacchati itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā.
segs.e: This is the seventh thing that pleases and assists an enemy which happens to an irritable woman or man.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, satta dhammā sapattakantā sapattakaraṇā kodhanaṁ āgacchanti itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vāti.
segs.e: These are the seven things that please and assist an enemy which happen to an irritable woman or man.
An irritable person is ugly
and they sleep badly.
When they get what they need,
they take it to be what they don’t need.
An angry person
kills with body or speech;
overcome with anger,
they lose their wealth.
Mad with anger,
they fall into disgrace.
Family, friends, and loved ones
avoid an irritable person.
Anger creates harm;
anger upsets the mind.
That person doesn’t recognize
the danger that arises within.
An angry person doesn’t know the good.
An angry person doesn’t see the truth.
When a person is beset by anger,
only blind darkness is left.
An angry person destroys with ease
what was hard to build.
Afterwards, when the anger is spent,
they’re tormented as if burnt by fire.
Their look betrays their sulkiness
like a fire’s smoky plume.
And when their anger flares up,
they make others angry.
They have no conscience or prudence,
nor any respectful speech.
One overcome by anger
has no island refuge anywhere.
The deeds that torment a man
are far from those that are good.
I’ll explain them now;
listen to this, for it is the truth.
An angry person slays their father;
their mother, too, they slay.
An angry person slays a saint;
a normal person, too, they slay.
A man is raised by his mother,
who shows him the world.
But an angry ordinary person slays
even that good woman who gave him life.
Like oneself, those sentient beings
hold themselves most dear.
But when angered, <j>they kill themselves in different ways,
distraught in many respects.
Some kill themselves with swords,
some, distraught, take poison.
Some hang themselves with rope,
or fling themselves down a mountain gorge.
When they commit deeds of baby-killing,
and killing themselves,
they don’t realize what they do,
for anger leads to their downfall.
The snare of death in the form of anger
lies hidden in the heart.
You should cut it out by self-control,
by wisdom, energy, and right ideas.
An astute person should cut out
this unskillful thing.
And they’d train in the teaching in just the same way,
not yielding to sulkiness.
Free of anger, free of despair,
free of greed, with no more longing,
tamed, having given up anger,
the undefiled are fully extinguished.”
Numbered Discourses 7.65
7. The Great Chapter
Conscience and Prudence

segs.p: “Hirottappe, bhikkhave, asati hirottappavipannassa hatūpaniso hoti indriyasaṁvaro;
segs.e: “Mendicants, when there is no conscience and prudence, one who lacks conscience and prudence has destroyed a vital condition for sense restraint.

segs.p: indriyasaṁvare asati indriyasaṁvaravipannassa hatūpanisaṁ hoti sīlaṁ;
segs.e: When there is no sense restraint, one who lacks sense restraint has destroyed a vital condition for ethical conduct.

segs.p: sīle asati sīlavipannassa hatūpaniso hoti sammāsamādhi;
segs.e: When there is no ethical conduct, one who lacks ethics has destroyed a vital condition for right immersion.

segs.p: sammāsamādhimhi asati sammāsamādhivipannassa hatūpanisaṁ hoti yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṁ;
segs.e: When there is no right immersion, one who lacks right immersion has destroyed a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

segs.p: yathābhūtañāṇadassane asati yathābhūtañāṇadassanavipannassa hatūpaniso hoti nibbidāvirāgo;
segs.e: When there is no true knowledge and vision, one who lacks true knowledge and vision has destroyed a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

segs.p: nibbidāvirāge asati nibbidāvirāgavipannassa hatūpanisaṁ hoti vimuttiñāṇadassanaṁ.
segs.e: When there is no disillusionment and dispassion, one who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.
Suppose there was a tree that lacked branches and foliage.

segs.p: Tassa papaṭikāpi na pāripūriṁ gacchati, tacopi pheggupi sāropi na pāripūriṁ gacchati.
segs.e: Its shoots, bark, softwood, and heartwood would not grow to fullness.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, hirottappe asati hirottappavipannassa hatūpaniso hoti indriyasaṁvaro;
segs.e: In the same way, when there is no conscience and prudence, a person who lacks conscience and prudence has destroyed a vital condition for sense restraint.

segs.p: indriyasaṁvare asati indriyasaṁvaravipannassa hatūpanisaṁ hoti sīlaṁ;
segs.e: When there is no sense restraint, one who lacks sense restraint has destroyed a vital condition for ethical conduct.

segs.p: sīle asati sīlavipannassa hatūpaniso hoti sammāsamādhi;
segs.e: When there is no ethical conduct, one who lacks ethics has destroyed a vital condition for right immersion.

segs.p: sammāsamādhimhi asati sammāsamādhivipannassa hatūpanisaṁ hoti yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṁ;
segs.e: When there is no right immersion, one who lacks right immersion has destroyed a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

segs.p: yathābhūtañāṇadassane asati yathābhūtañāṇadassanavipannassa hatūpaniso hoti nibbidāvirāgo;
segs.e: When there is no true knowledge and vision, one who lacks true knowledge and vision has destroyed a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

segs.p: nibbidāvirāge asati nibbidāvirāgavipannassa hatūpanisaṁ hoti vimuttiñāṇadassanaṁ.
segs.e: When there is no disillusionment and dispassion, one who lacks disillusionment and dispassion has destroyed a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

segs.p: Hirottappe, bhikkhave, sati hirottappasampannassa upanisasampanno hoti indriyasaṁvaro;
segs.e: When there is conscience and prudence, a person who has fulfilled conscience and prudence has fulfilled a vital condition for sense restraint.

segs.p: indriyasaṁvare sati indriyasaṁvarasampannassa upanisasampannaṁ hoti sīlaṁ;
segs.e: When there is sense restraint, one who has fulfilled sense restraint has fulfilled a vital condition for ethical conduct.

segs.p: sīle sati sīlasampannassa upanisasampanno hoti sammāsamādhi;
segs.e: When there is ethical conduct, one who has fulfilled ethical conduct has fulfilled a vital condition for right immersion.

segs.p: sammāsamādhimhi sati sammāsamādhisampannassa upanisasampannaṁ hoti yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṁ;
segs.e: When there is right immersion, one who has fulfilled right immersion has fulfilled a vital condition for true knowledge and vision.

segs.p: yathābhūtañāṇadassane sati yathābhūtañāṇadassanasampannassa upanisasampanno hoti nibbidāvirāgo;
segs.e: When there is true knowledge and vision, one who has fulfilled true knowledge and vision has fulfilled a vital condition for disillusionment and dispassion.

segs.p: nibbidāvirāge sati nibbidāvirāgasampannassa upanisasampannaṁ hoti vimuttiñāṇadassanaṁ.
segs.e: When there is disillusionment and dispassion, one who has fulfilled disillusionment and dispassion has fulfilled a vital condition for knowledge and vision of freedom.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, rukkho sākhāpalāsasampanno. Tassa papaṭikāpi pāripūriṁ gacchati, tacopi pheggupi sāropi pāripūriṁ gacchati.
segs.e: Suppose there was a tree that was complete with branches and foliage. Its shoots, bark, softwood, and heartwood would grow to fullness.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, hirottappe sati hirottappasampannassa upanisasampanno hoti …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, when there is conscience and prudence, one who has fulfilled conscience and prudence has fulfilled a vital condition for sense restraint. …
