segs.p: Tatonidānañhi so, bhikkhave, maraṇaṁ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṁ vā dukkhaṁ, na tveva tappaccayā kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjeyya.
segs.e: Because that might result in death or deadly pain. But when his body breaks up, after death, it would not cause him to be reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Yañca kho so, bhikkhave, dussīlo pāpadhammo …pe… kasambujāto khattiyamahāsālānaṁ vā brāhmaṇamahāsālānaṁ vā gahapatimahāsālānaṁ vā saddhādeyyaṁ vihāraṁ paribhuñjati. Tañhi tassa, bhikkhave, hoti dīgharattaṁ ahitāya dukkhāya kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: But when such an unethical man enjoys the use of dwellings given in faith by well-to-do aristocrats or brahmins or householders, that brings him lasting harm and suffering. When his body breaks up, after death, he’s reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.
So you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘yesañca mayaṁ paribhuñjāma cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṁ tesaṁ te kārā mahapphalā bhavissanti mahānisaṁsā, amhākañcevāyaṁ pabbajjā avañjhā bhavissati saphalā saudrayā’ti.
segs.e: ‘The services of those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick we enjoy shall be very fruitful and beneficial for them. And our going forth will not be barren, but will be fruitful and fertile.’
That’s how you should train.

segs.p: ‘attatthaṁ vā, bhikkhave, sampassamānena alameva appamādena sampādetuṁ;
segs.e: Considering what is good for yourself, mendicants, is quite enough for you to persist with diligence.

segs.p: paratthaṁ vā, bhikkhave, sampassamānena alameva appamādena sampādetuṁ;
segs.e: Considering what is good for others is quite enough for you to persist with diligence.

segs.p: ubhayatthaṁ vā, bhikkhave, sampassamānena alameva appamādena sampādetun’”ti.
segs.e: Considering what is good for both is quite enough for you to persist with diligence.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṁ bhaññamāne saṭṭhimattānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ uṇhaṁ lohitaṁ mukhato uggañchi.
segs.e: And while this discourse was being spoken, sixty monks spewed hot blood from their mouths.
Sixty mendicants resigned the training and returned to a lesser life, saying:
“It’s too hard, Blessed One! It’s just too hard!”

segs.p: Saṭṭhimattānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṁsūti.
segs.e: And sixty monks were freed from defilements by not grasping.
Numbered Discourses 7.73
7. The Great Chapter
About Sunetta

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sunetto nāma satthā ahosi titthakaro kāmesu vītarāgo.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, there was a teacher named Sunetta. He was a religious founder and was free of desire for sensual pleasures.

segs.p: Sunettassa kho pana, bhikkhave, satthuno anekāni sāvakasatāni ahesuṁ.
segs.e: He had many hundreds of disciples.

segs.p: Sunetto satthā sāvakānaṁ brahmalokasahabyatāya dhammaṁ desesi.
segs.e: He taught them a Dhamma for rebirth in the company of Divinity.

segs.p: Ye kho pana, bhikkhave, sunettassa satthuno brahmalokasahabyatāya dhammaṁ desentassa cittāni nappasādesuṁ te kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjiṁsu.
segs.e: Those lacking confidence in Sunetta were—when their body broke up, after death—reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Ye kho pana, bhikkhave, sunettassa satthuno brahmalokasahabyatāya dhammaṁ desentassa cittāni pasādesuṁ te kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjiṁsu.
segs.e: Those full of confidence in Sunetta were—when their body broke up, after death—reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, mūgapakkho nāma satthā ahosi …pe…
segs.e: Once upon a time, there was a teacher named Mūgapakkha …
Aranemi …
Kuddālaka …
Hatthipāla …
Jotipāla …

segs.p: arako nāma satthā ahosi titthakaro kāmesu vītarāgo.
segs.e: Araka. He was a religious founder and was free of desire for sensual pleasures.

segs.p: Arakassa kho pana, bhikkhave, satthuno anekāni sāvakasatāni ahesuṁ.
segs.e: He had many hundreds of disciples.

segs.p: Arako nāma satthā sāvakānaṁ brahmalokasahabyatāya dhammaṁ desesi.
segs.e: He taught them a Dhamma for rebirth in the company of Divinity.

segs.p: Ye kho pana, bhikkhave, arakassa satthuno brahmalokasahabyatāya dhammaṁ desentassa cittāni nappasādesuṁ, te kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjiṁsu.
segs.e: Those lacking confidence in Araka were—when their body broke up, after death—reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Ye kho pana, bhikkhave, arakassa satthuno brahmalokasahabyatāya dhammaṁ desentassa cittāni pasādesuṁ, te kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjiṁsu.
segs.e: Those full of confidence in Araka were—when their body broke up, after death—reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.
What do you think, mendicants?

segs.p: yo ime satta satthāre titthakare kāmesu vītarāge anekasataparivāre sasāvakasaṅghe paduṭṭhacitto akkoseyya paribhāseyya, bahuṁ so apuññaṁ pasaveyyā”ti?
segs.e: If someone with malicious intent were to abuse and insult these seven teachers with their hundreds of followers, would they not brim with much wickedness?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Yo, bhikkhave, ime satta satthāre titthakare kāmesu vītarāge anekasataparivāre sasāvakasaṅghe paduṭṭhacitto akkoseyya paribhāseyya, bahuṁ so apuññaṁ pasaveyya.
segs.e: “They would indeed.

segs.p: Yo ekaṁ diṭṭhisampannaṁ puggalaṁ paduṭṭhacitto akkosati paribhāsati, ayaṁ tato bahutaraṁ apuññaṁ pasavati.
segs.e: But someone who abuses and insults a single individual accomplished in view with malicious intent brims even more with wickedness.
Why is that?

segs.p: Nāhaṁ, bhikkhave, ito bahiddhā evarūpiṁ khantiṁ vadāmi yathāmaṁ sabrahmacārīsu.
segs.e: I say that any injury done by those outside of the Buddhist community does not compare with what is done to one’s own spiritual companions.
So you should train like this:
‘We will have no malicious intent for our spiritual companions.’
That’s how you should train.”
Numbered Discourses 7.74
7. The Great Chapter
About Araka

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, arako nāma satthā ahosi titthakaro kāmesu vītarāgo.
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, there was a teacher named Araka. He was a religious founder and was free of desire for sensual pleasures.

segs.p: Arakassa kho pana, bhikkhave, satthuno anekāni sāvakasatāni ahesuṁ.
segs.e: He had many hundreds of disciples,

segs.p: Arako satthā sāvakānaṁ evaṁ dhammaṁ deseti:
segs.e: and he taught them like this:

segs.p: ‘appakaṁ, brāhmaṇa, jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ lahukaṁ bahudukkhaṁ bahupāyāsaṁ mantāyaṁ boddhabbaṁ, kattabbaṁ kusalaṁ, caritabbaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, natthi jātassa amaraṇaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Brahmins, life as a human is short, brief, and fleeting, full of suffering and distress. Be thoughtful and wake up! Do what’s good and lead the spiritual life, for no one born can escape death.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, tiṇagge ussāvabindu sūriye uggacchante khippaṁyeva paṭivigacchati, na ciraṭṭhitikaṁ hoti;
segs.e: It’s like a drop of dew on a grass tip. When the sun comes up it vanishes right away and doesn’t last long.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, ussāvabindūpamaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ lahukaṁ bahudukkhaṁ bahupāyāsaṁ mantāyaṁ boddhabbaṁ, kattabbaṁ kusalaṁ, caritabbaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, natthi jātassa amaraṇaṁ.
segs.e: In the same way, life as a human is like a dewdrop. It’s brief and fleeting, full of suffering and distress. Be thoughtful and wake up! Do what’s good and lead the spiritual life, for no one born can escape death.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, thullaphusitake deve vassante udakabubbuḷaṁ khippaṁyeva paṭivigacchati, na ciraṭṭhitikaṁ hoti;
segs.e: It’s like when the heavens rain heavily. The bubbles vanish right away and don’t last long.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, udakabubbuḷūpamaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ lahukaṁ bahudukkhaṁ bahupāyāsaṁ mantāyaṁ boddhabbaṁ, kattabbaṁ kusalaṁ, caritabbaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, natthi jātassa amaraṇaṁ.
segs.e: In the same way, life as a human is like a bubble. …

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, udake daṇḍarāji khippaṁyeva paṭivigacchati, na ciraṭṭhitikā hoti;
segs.e: It’s like a line drawn in water. It vanishes right away and doesn’t last long.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, udake daṇḍarājūpamaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, life as a human is like a line drawn in water. …

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, nadī pabbateyyā dūraṅgamā sīghasotā hārahārinī, natthi so khaṇo vā layo vā muhutto vā yaṁ sā āvattati, atha kho sā gacchateva vattateva sandateva;
segs.e: It’s like a mountain river traveling far, flowing fast, carrying all before it. It doesn’t turn back—not for a moment, a second, an hour—but runs, rolls, and flows on.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, nadīpabbateyyūpamaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ lahukaṁ …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, life as a human is like a mountain river. …

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, balavā puriso jivhagge kheḷapiṇḍaṁ saṁyūhitvā akasireneva vameyya;
segs.e: It’s like a strong man who has formed a glob of spit on the tip of his tongue. He could easily spit it out.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, kheḷapiṇḍūpamaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, life as a human is like a glob of spit. …

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, divasaṁsantatte ayokaṭāhe maṁsapesi pakkhittā khippaṁyeva paṭivigacchati, na ciraṭṭhitikā hoti;
segs.e: Suppose there was an iron cauldron that had been heated all day. If you tossed a scrap of meat in, it would vanish right away and not last long.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, maṁsapesūpamaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ …pe…
segs.e: In the same way, life as a human is like a scrap of meat. …

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, gāvī vajjhā āghātanaṁ nīyamānā yaṁ yadeva pādaṁ uddharati, santikeva hoti vadhassa santikeva maraṇassa;
segs.e: It’s like a cow being led to the slaughterhouse. With every step she comes closer to the slaughter, closer to death.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, govajjhūpamaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ lahukaṁ bahudukkhaṁ bahupāyāsaṁ mantāyaṁ boddhabbaṁ, kattabbaṁ kusalaṁ, caritabbaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, natthi jātassa amaraṇan’ti.
segs.e: In the same way, life as a human is like a cow being slaughtered. It’s brief and fleeting, full of suffering and distress. Be thoughtful and wake up! Do what’s good and lead the spiritual life, for no one born can escape death.’

segs.p: Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena manussānaṁ saṭṭhivassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṁ ahosi, pañcavassasatikā kumārikā alaṁpateyyā ahosi.
segs.e: Now, mendicants, at that time human beings had a lifespan of 60,000 years. Girls could be married at 500 years of age.

segs.p: Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena manussānaṁ chaḷeva ābādhā ahesuṁ—
segs.e: And human beings only had six afflictions:

segs.p: sītaṁ, uṇhaṁ, jighacchā, pipāsā, uccāro, passāvo.
segs.e: cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the need to defecate and urinate.

segs.p: So hi nāma, bhikkhave, arako satthā evaṁ dīghāyukesu manussesu evaṁ ciraṭṭhitikesu evaṁ appābādhesu sāvakānaṁ evaṁ dhammaṁ desessati:
segs.e: But even though humans were so long-lived with so few afflictions, Araka still taught in this way:

segs.p: ‘appakaṁ, brāhmaṇa, jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ lahukaṁ bahudukkhaṁ bahupāyāsaṁ mantāyaṁ boddhabbaṁ, kattabbaṁ kusalaṁ, caritabbaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, natthi jātassa amaraṇan’ti.
segs.e: ‘Life as a human is short, brief, and fleeting, full of suffering and distress. Be thoughtful and wake up! Do what’s good and lead the spiritual life, for no one born can escape death.’

segs.p: Etarahi taṁ, bhikkhave, sammā vadamāno vadeyya:
segs.e: These days it’d be right to say:

segs.p: ‘appakaṁ jīvitaṁ manussānaṁ parittaṁ lahukaṁ bahudukkhaṁ bahupāyāsaṁ mantāyaṁ boddhabbaṁ, kattabbaṁ kusalaṁ, caritabbaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, natthi jātassa amaraṇan’ti.
segs.e: ‘Life as a human is short, brief, and fleeting, full of suffering and distress. Be thoughtful and wake up! Do what’s good and lead the spiritual life, for no one born can escape death.’

segs.p: Etarahi, bhikkhave, yo ciraṁ jīvati so vassasataṁ appaṁ vā bhiyyo.
segs.e: For these days a long life is a hundred years or a little more.

segs.p: Vassasataṁ kho pana, bhikkhave, jīvanto tīṇiyeva utusatāni jīvati—
segs.e: Living for a hundred years, there are just three hundred seasons,

segs.p: utusataṁ hemantānaṁ, utusataṁ gimhānaṁ, utusataṁ vassānaṁ.
segs.e: a hundred each of the winter, summer, and rains.

segs.p: Tīṇi kho pana, bhikkhave, utusatāni jīvanto dvādasayeva māsasatāni jīvati—
segs.e: Living for three hundred seasons, there are just twelve hundred months,

segs.p: cattāri māsasatāni hemantānaṁ, cattāri māsasatāni gimhānaṁ, cattāri māsasatāni vassānaṁ.
segs.e: four hundred in each of the winter, summer, and rains.

segs.p: Dvādasa kho pana, bhikkhave, māsasatāni jīvanto catuvīsatiyeva addhamāsasatāni jīvati—
segs.e: Living for twelve hundred months, there are just twenty-four hundred fortnights,

segs.p: aṭṭhaddhamāsasatāni hemantānaṁ, aṭṭhaddhamāsasatāni gimhānaṁ, aṭṭhaddhamāsasatāni vassānaṁ.
segs.e: eight hundred in each of the winter, summer, and rains.

segs.p: Catuvīsati kho pana, bhikkhave, addhamāsasatāni jīvanto chattiṁsaṁyeva rattisahassāni jīvati—
segs.e: Living for 2,400 fortnights, there are just 36,000 days,

segs.p: dvādasa rattisahassāni hemantānaṁ, dvādasa rattisahassāni gimhānaṁ, dvādasa rattisahassāni vassānaṁ.
segs.e: 12,000 in each of the summer, winter, and rains.

segs.p: Chattiṁsaṁ kho pana, bhikkhave, rattisahassāni jīvanto dvesattatiyeva bhattasahassāni bhuñjati—
segs.e: Living for 36,000 days, you just eat 72,000 meals,

segs.p: catuvīsati bhattasahassāni hemantānaṁ, catuvīsati bhattasahassāni gimhānaṁ, catuvīsati bhattasahassāni vassānaṁ saddhiṁ mātuthaññāya saddhiṁ bhattantarāyena.
segs.e: 24,000 in each of the summer, winter, and rains, including when you’re suckling at the breast, and when you’re prevented from eating.

segs.p: Tatrime bhattantarāyā kapimiddhopi bhattaṁ na bhuñjati, dukkhitopi bhattaṁ na bhuñjati, byādhitopi bhattaṁ na bhuñjati, uposathikopi bhattaṁ na bhuñjati, alābhakenapi bhattaṁ na bhuñjati.
segs.e: Things that prevent you from eating include anger, pain, sickness, sabbath, or being unable to get food.

segs.p: Iti kho, bhikkhave, mayā vassasatāyukassa manussassa āyupi saṅkhāto, āyuppamāṇampi saṅkhātaṁ, utūpi saṅkhātā, saṁvaccharāpi saṅkhātā, māsāpi saṅkhātā, addhamāsāpi saṅkhātā, rattipi saṅkhātā, divāpi saṅkhātā, bhattāpi saṅkhātā, bhattantarāyāpi saṅkhātā.
segs.e: So mendicants, for a human being with a hundred years lifespan I have counted the lifespan, the limit of the lifespan, the seasons, the years, the months, the fortnights, the nights, the days, the meals, and the things that prevent them from eating.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṁ sāvakānaṁ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṁ upādāya;
segs.e: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

segs.p: kataṁ vo taṁ mayā etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṁ vo amhākaṁ anusāsanī”ti.
segs.e: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, mendicants! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”
Numbered Discourses 7.75
8. The Monastic Law
An Expert in the Monastic Law (1st)

segs.p: “Sattahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo hoti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities is an expert in the monastic law.
What seven?
They know what is an offense.
They know what is not an offense.
They know what is a light offense.
They know what is a serious offense.

segs.p: sīlavā hoti pātimokkhasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu,
segs.e: They’re ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

segs.p: catunnaṁ jhānānaṁ ābhicetasikānaṁ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṁ nikāmalābhī hoti akicchalābhī akasiralābhī,
segs.e: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

segs.p: āsavānaṁ khayā anāsavaṁ cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, sattahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo hotī”ti.
segs.e: A mendicant with these seven qualities is an expert in the monastic law.”
Numbered Discourses 7.76
8. The Monastic Law
An Expert in the Monastic Law (2nd)

segs.p: “Sattahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo hoti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities is an expert in the monastic law.
What seven?
They know what is an offense.
They know what is not an offense.
They know what is a light offense.
They know what is a heavy offense.

segs.p: ubhayāni kho panassa pātimokkhāni vitthārena svāgatāni honti suvibhattāni suppavattīni suvinicchitāni suttaso anubyañjanaso,
segs.e: Both monastic codes have been passed down to them in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, well evaluated in both the rules and accompanying material.

segs.p: catunnaṁ jhānānaṁ ābhicetasikānaṁ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṁ nikāmalābhī hoti akicchalābhī akasiralābhī,
segs.e: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

segs.p: āsavānaṁ khayā anāsavaṁ cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, sattahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo hotī”ti.
segs.e: A mendicant with these seven qualities is an expert in the monastic law.”
Numbered Discourses 7.77
8. The Monastic Law
An Expert in the Monastic Law (3rd)

segs.p: “Sattahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo hoti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities is an expert in the monastic law.
What seven?
They know what is an offense.
They know what is not an offense.
They know what is a light offense.
They know what is a heavy offense.

segs.p: vinaye kho pana ṭhito hoti asaṁhīro,
segs.e: They’re firm and unfaltering in the training.

segs.p: catunnaṁ jhānānaṁ ābhicetasikānaṁ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṁ nikāmalābhī hoti akicchalābhī akasiralābhī,
segs.e: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in this life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.

segs.p: āsavānaṁ khayā anāsavaṁ cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, sattahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo hotī”ti.
segs.e: A mendicant with these seven qualities is an expert in the monastic law.”
Numbered Discourses 7.78
8. The Monastic Law
An Expert in the Monastic Law (4th)

segs.p: “Sattahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo hoti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities is an expert in the monastic law.
What seven?
They know what is an offense.
They know what is not an offense.
They know what is a light offense.
They know what is a heavy offense.

segs.p: anekavihitaṁ pubbenivāsaṁ anussarati, seyyathidaṁ—ekampi jātiṁ, dvepi jātiyo …pe… iti sākāraṁ sauddesaṁ anekavihitaṁ pubbenivāsaṁ anussarati.
segs.e: They recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details.

segs.p: Dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena yathākammūpage satte pajānāti.
segs.e: With clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.

segs.p: Āsavānaṁ khayā anāsavaṁ cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, sattahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo hotī”ti.
segs.e: A mendicant with these seven qualities is an expert in the monastic law.”
Numbered Discourses 7.79
8. The Monastic Law
Shines as an Expert in the Monastic Law (1st)
“Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities shines as an expert in the monastic law.
What seven?
They know what is an offense.
They know what is not an offense.
They know what is a light offense.
They know what is a heavy offense.
They’re ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places; seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken.

segs.p: catunnaṁ jhānānaṁ ābhicetasikānaṁ nikāmalābhī hoti akicchalābhī akasiralābhī,
segs.e: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.
They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, sattahi dhammehi samannāgato vinayadharo sobhatī”ti.
segs.e: A mendicant with these seven qualities shines as an expert in the monastic law.”
Numbered Discourses 7.80
8. The Monastic Law
Shines as an Expert in the Monastic Law (2nd)
“Mendicants, a mendicant with seven qualities shines as an expert in the monastic law.
What seven?
They know what is an offense.
They know what is not an offense.
They know what is a light offense.
They know what is a heavy offense.

segs.p: ubhayāni kho panassa pātimokkhāni vitthārena svāgatāni honti suvibhattāni suppavattīni suvinicchitāni suttaso anubyañjanaso,
segs.e: Both monastic codes have been passed down to them in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, well evaluated in both the rules and accompanying material.
They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.
They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, sattahi dhammehi samannāgato vinayadharo sobhatī”ti.
segs.e: A mendicant with these seven qualities shines as an expert in the monastic law.”
Numbered Discourses 7.81

They know what is an offense.

They know what is a light offense.
They know what is a serious offense.

segs.p: vinaye kho pana ṭhito hoti asaṁhīro,
segs.e: They’re firm and unfaltering in the training.
They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.
They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom, and live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

Numbered Discourses 7.83
8. The Monastic Law
The Teacher’s Instructions

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā upāli yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā upāli bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Upāli went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṁ desetu, yamahaṁ bhagavato dhammaṁ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyyan”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”
“Upāli, you might know that

segs.p: ‘ime dhammā na ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṁvattantī’ti;
segs.e: certain things don’t lead solely to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.
Categorically, you should remember these things as
not the teaching, not the training, and not the Teacher’s instructions.

segs.p: Ye ca kho tvaṁ, upāli, dhamme jāneyyāsi:
segs.e: You might know that

segs.p: ‘ime dhammā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṁvattantī’ti;
segs.e: certain things do lead solely to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, awakening, and extinguishment.
Categorically, you should remember these things as
the teaching, the training, and the Teacher’s instructions.”
Numbered Discourses 7.84
8. The Monastic Law
The Settling of Disciplinary Issues

segs.p: “Sattime, bhikkhave, adhikaraṇasamathā dhammā uppannuppannānaṁ adhikaraṇānaṁ samathāya vūpasamāya.
segs.e: “Mendicants, there are these seven principles for settling any disciplinary issues that might arise.
What seven?

segs.p: Sammukhāvinayo dātabbo, sativinayo dātabbo, amūḷhavinayo dātabbo, paṭiññātakaraṇaṁ dātabbaṁ, yebhuyyasikā dātabbā, tassapāpiyasikā dātabbā, tiṇavatthārako dātabbo.
segs.e: Resolution face-to-face to be applied. Resolution through recollection to be granted. Resolution because of past insanity to be granted. Acting according to what has been admitted. Majority decision. Further penalty. Covering over as if with grass.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, satta adhikaraṇasamathā dhammā uppannuppannānaṁ adhikaraṇānaṁ samathāya vūpasamāyā”ti.
segs.e: These are the seven principles for settling any disciplinary issues that might arise.”
Numbered Discourses 7.85
9. An Ascetic
A Mendicant
“Mendicants, it’s because of breaking seven things that you become a mendicant.
What seven?

segs.p: Sakkāyadiṭṭhi bhinnā hoti, vicikicchā bhinnā hoti, sīlabbataparāmāso bhinno hoti, rāgo bhinno hoti, doso bhinno hoti, moho bhinno hoti, māno bhinno hoti.
segs.e: Substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, greed, hate, delusion, and conceit.

segs.p: Imesaṁ kho, bhikkhave, sattannaṁ dhammānaṁ bhinnattā bhikkhu hotī”ti.
segs.e: It’s because of breaking these seven things that you become a mendicant.”
Numbered Discourses 7.86

“Mendicants, it’s because of quelling seven things that you become an ascetic …”

9. An Ascetic
A Perfected One
“Mendicants, it’s by being impeccably remote from seven things that you become a perfected one.
What seven?

segs.p: Sakkāyadiṭṭhi ārakā hoti, vicikicchā ārakā hoti, sīlabbataparāmāso ārako hoti, rāgo ārako hoti, doso ārako hoti, moho ārako hoti, māno ārako hoti.
segs.e: Substantialist view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, greed, hate, delusion, and conceit.

segs.p: Imesaṁ kho, bhikkhave, sattannaṁ dhammānaṁ ārakattā arahā hotī”ti.
segs.e: It’s because of being impeccably remote from these seven things that you become a perfected one.”
Numbered Discourses 7.93
9. An Ascetic
Bad Qualities
“Mendicants, there are these seven bad qualities.
What seven?

segs.p: Assaddho hoti, ahiriko hoti, anottappī hoti, appassuto hoti, kusīto hoti, muṭṭhassati hoti, duppañño hoti.
segs.e: Someone is faithless, shameless, imprudent, unlearned, lazy, unmindful, and witless.
These are the seven bad qualities.”
Numbered Discourses 7.94
9. An Ascetic
Good Qualities
“Mendicants, there are these seven good qualities.
What seven?

segs.p: Saddho hoti, hirīmā hoti, ottappī hoti, bahussuto hoti, āraddhavīriyo hoti, satimā hoti, paññavā hoti.
segs.e: Someone is faithful, conscientious, prudent, learned, energetic, mindful, and wise.
These are the seven good qualities.”
Numbered Discourses 7.95
10. Worthy of Offerings
Observing Impermanence in the Eye

segs.p: “Sattime, bhikkhave, puggalā āhuneyyā …pe… dakkhiṇeyyā añjalikaraṇīyā anuttaraṁ puññakkhettaṁ lokassa.
segs.e: “Mendicants, these seven individuals are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.
What seven?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo cakkhusmiṁ aniccānupassī viharati aniccasaññī aniccapaṭisaṁvedī satataṁ samitaṁ abbokiṇṇaṁ cetasā adhimuccamāno paññāya pariyogāhamāno.
segs.e: First, take an individual who meditates observing impermanence in the eye. They perceive impermanence and experience impermanence. Constantly, continually, and without interruption, they apply the mind and fathom with wisdom.

segs.p: So āsavānaṁ khayā anāsavaṁ cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: They realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements.

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho, bhikkhave, paṭhamo puggalo āhuneyyo pāhuneyyo …pe… anuttaraṁ puññakkhettaṁ lokassa.
segs.e: This is the first individual who is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, idhekacco puggalo cakkhusmiṁ aniccānupassī viharati aniccasaññī aniccapaṭisaṁvedī satataṁ samitaṁ abbokiṇṇaṁ cetasā adhimuccamāno paññāya pariyogāhamāno.
segs.e: Next, take an individual who meditates observing impermanence in the eye. …

segs.p: Tassa apubbaṁ acarimaṁ āsavapariyādānañca hoti jīvitapariyādānañca.
segs.e: Their defilements and their life come to an end at exactly the same time.

segs.p: Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, dutiyo puggalo āhuneyyo …pe… anuttaraṁ puññakkhettaṁ lokassa.
segs.e: This is the second individual who is worthy of offerings …

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, idhekacco puggalo cakkhusmiṁ aniccānupassī viharati aniccasaññī aniccapaṭisaṁvedī satataṁ samitaṁ abbokiṇṇaṁ cetasā adhimuccamāno paññāya pariyogāhamāno.
segs.e: Next, take an individual who meditates observing impermanence in the eye. …

segs.p: So pañcannaṁ orambhāgiyānaṁ saṁyojanānaṁ parikkhayā antarāparinibbāyī hoti …pe…
segs.e: With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished between one life and the next. …
With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished upon landing. …
With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished without extra effort. …
With the ending of the five lower fetters they’re extinguished with extra effort. …
With the ending of the five lower fetters they head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm. …

segs.p: Ayaṁ, bhikkhave, sattamo puggalo āhuneyyo …pe… anuttaraṁ puññakkhettaṁ lokassa.
segs.e: This is the seventh individual.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, satta puggalā āhuneyyā pāhuneyyā dakkhiṇeyyā añjalikaraṇīyā anuttaraṁ puññakkhettaṁ lokassā”ti.
segs.e: These are the seven individuals who are worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and are the supreme field of merit for the world.”
Numbered Discourses 7.96–614

11. Abbreviated Texts Beginning With Greed
Untitled Discourse on Greed (1st)
“Mendicants, for insight into greed, seven things should be developed.
What seven?
The awakening factor of mindfulness …
the awakening factor of equanimity.

segs.p: rāgassa, bhikkhave, abhiññāya ime satta dhammā bhāvetabbā”ti.
segs.e: These seven things should be developed for insight into greed.”
Numbered Discourses 7.616
11. Abbreviated Texts Beginning With Greed
Untitled Discourse on Greed (2nd)
“Mendicants, for insight into greed, seven things should be developed.
What seven?

segs.p: Aniccasaññā, anattasaññā, asubhasaññā, ādīnavasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññā, nirodhasaññā—
segs.e: The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of ugliness, the perception of drawbacks, the perception of giving up, the perception of fading away, and the perception of cessation.

segs.p: rāgassa, bhikkhave, abhiññāya ime satta dhammā bhāvetabbā”ti.
segs.e: These seven things should be developed for insight into greed.”
Numbered Discourses 7.617
11. Abbreviated Texts Beginning With Greed
Untitled Discourse on Greed (3rd)
“Mendicants, for insight into greed, seven things should be developed.
What seven?

segs.p: Asubhasaññā, maraṇasaññā, āhāre paṭikūlasaññā, sabbaloke anabhiratasaññā, aniccasaññā, anicce dukkhasaññā, dukkhe anattasaññā—
segs.e: The perceptions of ugliness, death, repulsiveness of food, dissatisfaction with the whole world, impermanence, suffering in impermanence, and not-self in suffering.

segs.p: rāgassa, bhikkhave, abhiññāya ime satta dhammā bhāvetabbā”ti.
segs.e: These seven things should be developed for insight into greed.”

segs.p: Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṁ abhinandunti.
segs.e: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.
The Book of the Sevens is finished.
